chain.g: letter of the alphabet"; in plural, "epistle

ety.text: From Middle English letter, lettre, from Old French letre, from Latin littera (“letter of the alphabet"; in plural, "epistle”). Displaced Old English bōcstæf (literally “book staff”) in sense 1 and ǣrendġewrit (literally “message writing”) in sense 2.
From Middle English letere, equivalent to let + -er.

senses.d: A symbol in an alphabet.
ex: There are twenty-six letters in the English alphabet.
And a superscription also was written ouer him in letters of Greeke, and Latin, & Hebrew, THIS IS THE KING OF THE IEWES.

senses.d: A written or printed communication, usually defined as longer and more formal than a note. (Sometimes specifically one that is on paper.)
ex: I wrote a letter to my sister about my life.
The style of letters ought to be free, easy, and natural.

senses.d: The literal meaning of something, as distinguished from its intended and remoter meaning (the spirit).
ex: I broke the letter of it to keep the sense.
Some MEPs from some countries may have pocketed £2m more than I have by observing the letter but not the spirit of the rules.

senses.d: Literature.
ex: Benjamin Franklin was multiskilled – a scientist, politician and a man of letters.

senses.d: A division unit of a piece of law marked by a letter of the alphabet.
ex: Letter (b) constitutes an exception to this provision.

senses.d: A size of paper, 8½ in × 11 in (215.9 mm × 279.4 mm).
A size of paper, 215 mm × 280 mm.
A single type; type, collectively; a style of type.
ex: Under these, thro’ a garden in which is an ample fountaine, was the King's printing-house, and that famous letter so much esteem’d.

senses.d: To print, inscribe, or paint letters on something.
To earn a varsity letter (award).
ex: I think Mom lettered in shot put her junior year.

senses.d: One who lets, or lets out.
ex: the letter of a room
a blood-letter

senses.d: One who retards or hinders.

chain.g: to allow, let go, bequeath, leave, rent

ety.text: Derived from Middle English leten, læten, from Old English lǣtan (“to allow, let go, bequeath, leave, rent”), from Proto-West Germanic *lātan, from Proto-Germanic *lētaną (“to leave behind, allow”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁d- (“to be tired, leave”).

chain.g: to hinder, delay”; literally, “to make late

ety.text: Derived from Middle English letten (“to hinder, delay”), from Old English lettan (“to hinder, delay”; literally, “to make late”), from Proto-West Germanic *lattjan, from Proto-Germanic *latjaną. Akin to Old English latian (“to delay”), Dutch letten, Old English læt (“late”). More at late, delay.

senses.d: To allow to, not to prevent (+ infinitive, but usually without to).
ex: After he knocked for hours, I decided to let him come in.
I never let myself worry about the future.

senses.d: To allow to be or do without interference; to not disturb or meddle with; to leave alone.
ex: Let me be!
Yet neither spinnes nor cardes, ne cares nor frets, / But to her mother Nature all her care she lets.

senses.d: To allow the release of (a fluid).
ex: The physicians let about a pint of his blood, but to no avail.

senses.d: To allow possession of (a property etc.) in exchange for rent.
ex: I decided to let the farmhouse to a couple while I was working abroad.
Trailers for sale or rent, rooms to let, fifty cents.

senses.d: To give, grant, or assign, as a work, privilege, or contract; often with out.
ex: to let the building of a bridge;  to let out the lathing and the plastering

senses.d: Used to introduce a first or third person imperative verb construction.
ex: Let's put on a show!
Let us have a moment of silence.

senses.d: To cause (+ bare infinitive).
ex: Can you let me know what time you'll be arriving?
Time's sea hath been five years at its slow ebb, / Long hours have to and fro let creep the sand[…].

senses.d: The allowing of possession of a property etc. in exchange for rent.
ex:
Then he says “You would call it a Good Let, Madam?”
“O certainly a Good Let sir.”

senses.d: To hinder, prevent, impede, hamper, cumber; to obstruct (someone or something).
ex: He who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way.
Sir King, mine ancient wound is hardly whole, / And lets me from the saddle; […]

senses.d: To prevent someone from doing something; also to prevent something from happening.
To tarry or delay.
ex: And for that strake I would not let, / Another upon him soon I set, […]

senses.d: An obstacle or hindrance.
ex: without let or hindrance
[E]ver conſider vvhether our doings be to the let of our ſalvation or not.
